description: Spider mites are common pests of fruit trees, vegetables, berries, vines, houseplants, and ornamental plants. Mites are tiny arachnids with eight legs, related to spiders and ticks.
identification: Adults are less than 1/20 inch long with an oval body and two colored eyespots near the head
Live in colonies, mostly on the underside of leaves; a single colony can contain hundreds of mites
High populations produce dense webbing covering leaves, twigs, and fruit
Look for stippling of light dots on leaves, bronze discoloration, yellowing, and leaf drop
damage: Suck cell contents from leaves, causing stippling and discoloration
Severely infested leaves turn yellow and may drop
Damage is most severe in hot, dusty conditions and on water-stressed plants
natural_enemies: Predatory mites (larger with longer legs and more active)
management: Water plants to avoid drought stress
Reduce dust using ground covers, mulches, and regular irrigation
Encourage natural enemies to control populations
Spray water or mist on the undersides of leaves daily if infested
chemical_control: Insecticidal oils or insecticidal soaps, applied thoroughly on undersides of leaves
Avoid spraying when plants are water-stressed or during high heat
Avoid insecticides that kill natural enemies, as these can cause mite population spikes
notes: Spider mites frequently become problematic after certain organophosphate or pyrethroid insecticide applications
Minimize pesticide use, prefer nonchemical or less toxic options
Read product labels carefully for proper usage and disposal
